title: Inside and outside
hookLine: the refrain: in oneself, in others, both; arising and passing away (MN 10)

lines: THE VERSES SAY WHERE; THE CHORUS SAYS HOW.
cards: Some songs have a chorus that comes back after every verse, and by the end you're singing it without thinking. The Satipatthana Sutta works like that.
After every exercise, the breath, the postures, the parts of the body, feelings, the mind, all of it, the same few lines come back. It's easy to skip them as repetition.
But some teachers call the chorus the heart of the whole sutta. The verses tell you where to look. The chorus tells you how.

teach.b: Here's the chorus, in plain words.
The practitioner contemplates the body as a body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

They contemplate its nature of arising, its nature of passing away, and both arising and passing away. Or else mindfulness that there is a body is simply present, just enough for knowing and for continued mindfulness.
And they live independent, not clinging to anything in the world. Three pieces. First, inside and outside.
Internally means in yourself. Externally is usually explained as in others: the same breath, the same body, the same moods in the person across from you.

Commentators and modern teachers read this line a few different ways, and the text doesn't settle it. One reading: what you learn in your own body helps you understand everyone else's. Second, arising and passing away.
Whatever you watch, a breath, an itch, a mood, you see it come and go. Watched closely, nothing in it holds still for long.
This is the doorway to what Buddhists call impermanence, anicca, not as an idea, but as something you watch happen. Third, independent, not clinging.

teach.h: JUST ENOUGH TO KNOW, CLINGING TO NOTHING.
teach.b: The knowing is just enough to know.
It doesn't grab, doesn't build a story, doesn't need the breath to stay a certain way. Three moves, after every exercise, until they become the way you look at everything.

how: In insight meditation traditions, practitioners return to the sutta's refrain after each exercise: seeing the body, feelings and mind in themselves and in others, and watching them arise and pass away without clinging.

o: impermanence: everything arises and passes away
the idea that the soul lives on forever
a sad belief that nothing in life matters

games.q: match each piece of the chorus.

s: the chorus is repeated only once, at the end of the sutta
it comes back after every exercise, like a song's chorus.
it's usually read as 'in others', but commentators and teachers read it in more than one way.
watching arising and passing is a doorway to impermanence
anicca, seen happening, not just thought about.

games.q: you're watching an itch on your arm. the chorus says to see its arising and passing. what do you do?
o: watch it rise, shift and fade, without grabbing or fighting.
decide it will never go away.
games.why: the chorus asks you to watch things come and go, knowing just enough to know, not clinging.

practice: Pick one small sensation, the breath at the nostrils, warmth in the hands, a pressure where you sit, and watch it arise, shift, fade and arise again; nothing in it holds still.
Then, for a breath or two, remember that every person around you right now has a body doing the same. Inside, outside, arising, passing: just enough to know.

wordCard.voice: Anicca. The sutta's chorus, watched inside yourself and in others: everything arising, everything passing away.

orig.note: Pali anicca: impermanence, seen in the chorus as arising and passing away.

carryVoice: Your line: it arises, it passes. Inside you, and in everyone else. Two hundred fifty, done.
